3.1.1.title: Topic 3.1.1 · Atomic Structure
3.1.1.spec: Fundamental particles, mass number, isotopes, TOF mass spectrometry, electron configuration, ionisation energies

sections.heading: Fundamental Particles & Isotopes
points: Fundamental particles: Proton (mass 1, charge +1), Neutron (mass 1, charge 0), Electron (mass 1/1840, charge -1).
Atomic number (Z): Number of protons in nucleus. Defines the chemical identity of the element.
Mass number (A): Total number of protons + neutrons in nucleus.
Isotopes: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Chemical properties are identical because they have the exact same electron configuration.
Relative atomic mass (Ar): The weighted average mass of an atom of an element compared with 1/12th of the mass of an atom of Carbon-12.

sections.heading: Time of Flight (TOF) Mass Spectrometry
points: 1. Ionisation:

• Electron impact: Vaporised sample bombarded by high-energy electrons from an electron gun; knocks off one electron: X(g) → X+(g) + e−. Used for elements and substances with low Mr; can cause fragmentation.

• Electrospray ionisation: Sample dissolved in volatile solvent and injected through a fine hypodermic needle at high positive voltage; gains a proton: X(g) + H+ → XH+(g). Soft ionisation, no fragmentation; Mr is m/z − 1.
2. Acceleration: Positive ions accelerated by an electric field so all ions have the SAME kinetic energy (KE = ½mv2).
3. Ion drift: Ions enter a flight tube with no electric field. Velocity depends on mass (v = √(2KE/m)). Lighter ions travel faster and have a shorter time of flight (t = d√(m / 2KE)).
4. Detection: Positive ions hit a negatively charged detector plate, gain electrons, and generate an electric current. Size of current is proportional to abundance.

sections.heading: Electron Configuration & Ionisation Energies
points: Orbitals & Sub-shells: Orbitals hold up to 2 electrons with opposite spins. Sub-shells: s (1 orbital, 2e), p (3 orbitals, 6e), d (5 orbitals, 10e).
Filling order: 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p. 4s fills before 3d and 4s electrons are lost first during ionisation.
Exceptions to know: Chromium: [Ar] 4s1 3d5 (half-filled d sub-shell stability); Copper: [Ar] 4s1 3d10 (fully-filled d sub-shell stability).
First Ionisation Energy (IE): Enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is removed from 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous 1+ ions: X(g) → X+(g) + e−.
General Period 3 trend: Increases across period due to increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding.
Period 3 anomalies:
• Mg to Al drop: Al loses electron from 3p subshell, which is higher in energy and shielded by 3s electrons.
• P to S drop: S has paired electrons in a 3p orbital; repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove.

3.1.2.title: Topic 3.1.2 · Amount of Substance
3.1.2.spec: Avogadro constant, mole calculations, ideal gas equation, empirical/molecular formulas, atom economy, percentage yield, titrations

sections.heading: The Mole & Key Calculation Formulas
points: Avogadro constant (L or NA): 6.022 × 1023 mol−1 (number of entities in 1 mole of substance).
Mass formula: n = m / Mr (m in grams, Mr in g mol−1).
Solution formula: n = c × V (c in mol dm−3, V in dm3; divide cm3 by 1000).
Mass concentration: conc (g dm−3) = conc (mol dm−3) × Mr.

sections.heading: Ideal Gas Equation (pV = nRT)
points: Equation: pV = nRT where R = 8.31 J K−1 mol−1.
SI Unit conversions (essential):
• Pressure p: in Pa (kPa × 1000 = Pa; MPa × 106 = Pa).
• Volume V: in m3 (dm3 × 10−3 = m3; cm3 × 10−6 = m3).
• Temperature T: in Kelvin (K) (°C + 273).
Finding Mr of volatile liquid: Mr = (m × R × T) / (p × V).

sections.heading: Empirical Formula, Yield & Atom Economy
points: Empirical formula: Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. Calculate moles (mass / Ar), divide by smallest mole value to find ratio.
Molecular formula: Actual number of atoms of each element. Scale factor = Mr / empirical mass.
Percentage yield: (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) × 100%. (Reduced by incomplete reaction, reversible equilibria, side reactions, purification losses).
Percentage atom economy: (Mr of desired product / Total Mr of all reactants) × 100%. Industrial importance: minimizes waste, conserves raw materials, lowers cost.

Titrations & Concordancy: Concordant titres are within ±0.10 cm3 of each other. Only average concordant titres. Standard volumetric uncertainty calculation: percentage uncertainty = (uncertainty / reading) × 100%.

3.1.3.title: Topic 3.1.3 · Bonding & Structure
3.1.3.spec: Ionic, covalent, dative covalent, metallic bonding, 4 crystal structures, VSEPR shapes, electronegativity, intermolecular forces

sections.heading: Types of Bonding & 4 Crystal Structures
points: Ionic bonding: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice (e.g. NaCl, MgO). High mp, brittle, conducts electricity only when molten or aqueous.
Covalent bonding: Shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms.
Dative (co-ordinate) bond: Covalent bond where both shared electrons are donated by one atom (e.g. NH4+, H3O+, [AlCl4]−, CO). Shown by an arrow from donor to acceptor.
Metallic bonding: Attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised sea of electrons (e.g. Mg, Na). High electrical and thermal conductivity, malleable, ductile.
4 Crystal types:
• Giant ionic: NaCl (each Na+ surrounded by 6 Cl−).

• Macromolecular: Diamond (each C bonded tetrahedrally to 4 others, extremely hard, non-conductor); Graphite (hexagonal layers bonded to 3 C, delocalised electrons conduct, weak van der Waals between layers allow sliding - lubricant); Ice (open hexagonal hydrogen-bonded lattice, density of ice < liquid water).
• Molecular: Iodine (I2 molecules held by weak London dispersion forces, sublimes easily).
• Giant metallic: Magnesium lattice of Mg2+ ions with 2 delocalised electrons per atom.

sections.heading: VSEPR Shapes of Molecules & Bond Angles
points: VSEPR Principle: Electron pairs repel to maximum separation. Repulsion order: Lone pair - lone pair > Lone pair - bond pair > Bond pair - bond pair. Each lone pair reduces bond angle by approx 2.5°.
• 2 pairs: Linear (180°, e.g. BeCl2, CO2).
• 3 pairs (0 lp): Trigonal planar (120°, e.g. BF3, AlCl3).
• 4 pairs (0 lp): Tetrahedral (109.5°, e.g. CH4, NH4+).
• 4 pairs (1 lp): Trigonal pyramidal (107°, e.g. NH3, H3O+).
• 4 pairs (2 lp): Bent / V-shaped (104.5°, e.g. H2O, H2S, NH2−).
• 5 pairs (0 lp): Trigonal bipyramidal (90° and 120°, e.g. PCl5).
• 6 pairs (0 lp): Octahedral (90°, e.g. SF6, [Fe(H2O)6]2+).
• 6 pairs (2 lp): Square planar (90°, e.g. XeF4, [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]).

sections.heading: Electronegativity & Intermolecular Forces
points: Electronegativity: The power of an atom to attract the electron density in a covalent bond towards itself. Increases across periods and decreases down groups (F > O > N > Cl).

Permanent dipole: Arises when two bonded atoms have differing electronegativities (Δχ > 0.4). Symmetrical molecules (e.g. CCl4, CO2, BF3) have polar bonds but no overall dipole because dipoles cancel out.
Intermolecular forces (weakest to strongest):
1. van der Waals / London dispersion: Induced dipole-dipole interactions due to temporary uneven electron distribution. Increases with number of electrons / molecular size.
2. Permanent dipole-dipole: Electrostatic attraction between polar molecules (e.g. HCl, CH3Cl).
3. Hydrogen bonding: Attraction between lone pair on strongly electronegative atom (N, O, F) and an electron-deficient H atom bonded to N, O, or F. Explains anomalous high bp of H2O, HF, NH3.

3.1.4.title: Topic 3.1.4 · Energetics
3.1.4.spec: Enthalpy changes, standard enthalpy of formation and combustion, calorimetry, Hess's Law, mean bond enthalpies

sections.heading: Standard Enthalpy Definitions
points: Enthalpy change (ΔH): Heat energy change measured under constant pressure conditions. Exothermic (ΔH < 0), Endothermic (ΔH > 0).
Standard conditions: 100 kPa pressure and stated temperature (usually 298 K / 25°C).

Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔfH°): Enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states under standard conditions. ΔfH° for any element in its standard state is ZERO.
Standard enthalpy of combustion (ΔcH°): Enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance burns completely in excess oxygen under standard conditions.

sections.heading: Calorimetry & Calculations
points: Heat energy equation: q = mcΔT (q in Joules, m is mass of solution in grams, c = 4.18 J g−1 K−1, ΔT in K or °C).
Molar enthalpy: ΔH = − (q / 1000) / n (in kJ mol−1). Always include sign (− for exothermic, + for endothermic)!
Sources of error: Heat loss to surroundings, incomplete combustion, non-standard conditions, evaporation of fuel.
Cooling curve correction: Plot temperature against time before, during, and after mixing. Extrapolate cooling line back to time of mixing to find true theoretical ΔT.

sections.heading: Hess's Law & Mean Bond Enthalpies
points: Hess's Law: Total enthalpy change for a chemical reaction is independent of the route taken.
• From enthalpies of formation: ΔHr = ∑ ΔfH(products) − ∑ ΔfH(reactants).
• From enthalpies of combustion: ΔHr = ∑ ΔcH(reactants) − ∑ ΔcH(products).
Mean bond enthalpy: Enthalpy change needed to break 1 mole of a covalent bond into gaseous atoms, averaged over a wide range of different compounds.
Bond enthalpy formula: ΔH = ∑ (bonds broken) − ∑ (bonds formed) (reactants − products).

Discrepancy reason: Calculations using mean bond enthalpies are approximations because they use average values from multiple compounds, whereas Hess's law uses specific experimental standard enthalpy data for that exact compound in its actual physical state.

3.1.5.title: Topic 3.1.5 · Kinetics
3.1.5.spec: Collision theory, activation energy, Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions, factors affecting reaction rate, catalysts

sections.heading: Collision Theory & Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
points: Collision theory: Reactions occur when reacting particles collide with kinetic energy ≥ activation energy (Ea) and with correct collision orientation.
Activation Energy (Ea): The minimum energy required for colliding particles to react.
Maxwell-Boltzmann curve features:
• Starts at origin (no molecules have zero energy).
• Peak represents most probable energy (Emp).
• Mean energy is to the right of the peak.
• Asymptotic: never touches x-axis at high energies (no theoretical maximum energy).
• Total area under curve equals total number of gas molecules.

sections.heading: Effect of Temperature, Concentration & Catalysts
points: Effect of higher temperature:
• Curve peak shifts to the right and lowers; distribution broadens.
• Area under curve remains constant.
• A significantly larger fraction of molecules have energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub>.
• Collision frequency increases slightly, but the main factor causing rapid rate increase is the greater proportion of successful collisions.
Effect of concentration / pressure: More particles per unit volume → collision frequency increases → rate increases proportionally.

Catalysts: Increase the rate of reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. Catalyst is unchanged at end. On Maxwell-Boltzmann, Ea line shifts to the left, meaning a greater fraction of molecules have energy ≥ Ecat.

3.1.6.title: Topic 3.1.6 · Chemical Equilibria & Kc
3.1.6.spec: Dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle, industrial compromises, equilibrium constant Kc

sections.heading: Dynamic Equilibrium & Le Chatelier's Principle
points: Dynamic equilibrium conditions: Closed system; forward and reverse reactions proceed at the exact same rate; concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
Le Chatelier's Principle: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in conditions, the position of equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes that change.
• Temperature increase: Shifts in the endothermic direction (ΔH > 0) to absorb heat.
• Temperature decrease: Shifts in the exothermic direction (ΔH < 0) to release heat.
• Pressure increase: Shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas to reduce pressure.
• Catalyst: Increases rates of forward and reverse reactions equally. Does NOT change equilibrium position or yield; reaches equilibrium faster.

sections.heading: Equilibrium Constant (Kc)
points: For homogeneous reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD:
Kc expression: Kc = ([C]c [D]d) / ([A]a [B]b) where square brackets denote equilibrium concentration in mol dm−3.
Units: Work out by substituting (mol dm−3) into expression and cancelling out powers.
Crucial rule: ONLY TEMPERATURE alters the value of Kc. Changes in concentration, pressure, or adding a catalyst do NOT alter Kc.
• For exothermic reaction: increasing T shifts equilibrium left → Kc decreases.
• For endothermic reaction: increasing T shifts equilibrium right → Kc increases.

3.1.7.title: Topic 3.1.7 · Oxidation, Reduction & Redox Equations
3.1.7.spec: Oxidation states, electron transfer, half-equations, combining redox equations

sections.heading: Oxidation States & Redox Definitions
points: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; Reduction Is Gain of electrons.
Oxidising agent: Electron acceptor (gets reduced itself; causes oxidation).
Reducing agent: Electron donor (gets oxidised itself; causes reduction).
Oxidation state rules:
• Uncombined elements = 0.
• Neutral compounds sum to 0; polyatomic ions sum to overall ionic charge.
• Group 1 metals = +1; Group 2 = +2; Aluminium = +3.
• Fluorine is always −1.
• Oxygen is −2 (except in peroxides H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> where it is −1, and in OF<sub>2</sub> where it is +2).
• Hydrogen is +1 (except in metal hydrides NaH where it is −1).
• Chlorine is −1 (except in compounds with F or O e.g. ClO<sup>−</sup> where Cl is +1).

sections.heading: Balancing Redox Half-Equations
points: Step-by-step method:
1. Balance atoms other than H and O.
2. Balance oxygen atoms by adding H<sub>2</sub>O molecules.
3. Balance hydrogen atoms by adding H<sup>+</sup> ions.
4. Balance electric charge by adding electrons (e<sup>−</sup>).
Key half-equations:
• Manganate(VII) reduction: MnO4− + 8H+ + 5e− → Mn2+ + 4H2O.
• Dichromate(VI) reduction: Cr2O72− + 14H+ + 6e− → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O.
• Ethanedioate oxidation: C2O42− → 2CO2 + 2e−.
• Iron(II) oxidation: Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e−.
• Hydrogen peroxide: H2O2 → O2 + 2H+ + 2e−.

3.1.8.title: Topic 3.1.8 · Thermodynamics (A-Level)
3.1.8.spec: Born-Haber cycles, lattice enthalpy, entropy change, Gibbs free energy, feasibility

sections.heading: Born-Haber Cycles & Lattice Enthalpy
points: Lattice enthalpy of formation: Enthalpy change when 1 mole of a solid ionic compound is formed from its constituent gaseous ions under standard conditions (always EXOTHERMIC, negative).
Lattice enthalpy of dissociation: Enthalpy change when 1 mole of a solid ionic compound is completely separated into its gaseous ions (always ENDOTHERMIC, positive).
Cycle enthalpy steps: Formation = Atomisation + Ionisation energies + Electron affinities + Lattice formation.

Electron affinity: 1st EA is exothermic (negative) because incoming electron is attracted by nucleus; 2nd EA (e.g. O− + e− → O2−) is always ENDOTHERMIC (positive) due to strong repulsion between negative ion and incoming electron.

Born-Haber vs Perfect Ionic Model: If experimental (Born-Haber) lattice enthalpy is significantly more exothermic than the theoretical value calculated assuming point charges (perfect ionic model), the compound has significant covalent character caused by cation polarisation.

sections.heading: Entropy & Gibbs Free Energy
points: Entropy (S): Measure of disorder of a system (in J K−1 mol−1). S(gas) >> S(liquid) > S(solid).
ΔS calculation: ΔS = ∑ S°(products) − ∑ S°(reactants).
Gibbs Free Energy Equation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (ΔH in kJ mol−1, T in Kelvin, ΔS must be converted to kJ K−1 mol−1 by dividing by 1000!).
Feasibility: Reaction is feasible when ΔG ≤ 0.
Feasibility temperature: T = ΔH / ΔS (at ΔG = 0).
ΔG vs T graph: ΔG = −ΔS(T) + ΔH. Gradient = −ΔS, y-intercept = ΔH.

3.1.9.title: Topic 3.1.9 · Rate Equations & Arrhenius (A-Level)
3.1.9.spec: Rate equations, orders of reaction, rate constant, rate-determining step, Arrhenius equation

sections.heading: Rate Equations & Orders of Reaction
points: Rate equation: Rate = k[A]m[B]n where m and n are reaction orders (0, 1, or 2), and k is rate constant.
• Zero order (m = 0): Concentration has NO effect on rate. Rate = k. [A]-time graph is linear downward slope.
• First order (m = 1): Rate is directly proportional to [A]. Constant half-life t½.
• Second order (m = 2): Doubling [A] quadruples the rate (22 = 4).
Units of k: Units = (mol dm−3 s−1) / [concentration units]overall order. E.g. 1st order: s−1; 2nd order: mol−1 dm3 s−1; 3rd order: mol−2 dm6 s−1.
Rate Determining Step (RDS): The slowest step in a reaction mechanism. Species appearing in the rate equation must participate in the RDS or steps preceding it.

sections.heading: The Arrhenius Equation
points: Equation: k = A e−Ea / RT.
Logarithmic form: ln k = −(Ea / R)(1/T) + ln A.
Graphical analysis: Plot ln k (y-axis) against 1/T (x-axis, in K−1).
• Gradient = −Ea / R → Ea = −gradient × 8.31 J mol−1 (divide by 1000 for kJ mol−1).
• y-intercept = ln A → A = eintercept.

3.1.10.title: Topic 3.1.10 · Equilibrium Constant Kp (A-Level)
3.1.10.spec: Mole fractions, partial pressures, expressions for Kp, calculation of Kp, effect of temperature and pressure

sections.heading: Mole Fractions & Partial Pressures
points: Mole fraction (xA): xA = (moles of gas A) / (total moles of all gases). Sum of mole fractions = 1.0.
Partial pressure (pA): pA = xA × Ptotal.
Total pressure: Ptotal = ∑ pi (Dalton's Law).

sections.heading: Kp Expressions & Temperature Effect
points: For aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g):
Kp expression: Kp = (pCc × pDd) / (pAa × pBb). Use round brackets and partial pressures, NOT square concentration brackets!
Kp Units: Substitute pressure unit (kPa or Pa) and cancel.
Key principles:
• ONLY temperature changes Kp.
• Changing pressure causes the system to adjust partial pressures so the quotient returns to the constant Kp value at that temperature.
• Adding a catalyst has NO effect on Kp or position of equilibrium.

3.1.11.title: Topic 3.1.11 · Electrode Potentials & Cells (A-Level)
3.1.11.spec: Standard hydrogen electrode, IUPAC cell conventions, EMF calculations, commercial cells, fuel cells

sections.heading: Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) & Cell Conventions
points: Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE): Reference electrode assigned 0.00 V under standard conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa H2 gas, 1.00 mol dm−3 H+ ions, platinised Pt electrode (inert catalyst).
IUPAC Cell Convention:
• Single line | indicates phase boundary (e.g. solid to aqueous).
• Double line || indicates salt bridge (filter paper soaked in saturated KNO<sub>3</sub> or KCl).
• Left electrode is oxidation (more negative E°); Right electrode is reduction (more positive E°).
• Example: Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq) || Cu2+(aq) | Cu(s).
EMF Calculation: E°cell = E°right − E°left. Reaction is feasible if E°cell > 0.

sections.heading: Commercial Cells & Hydrogen Fuel Cells
points: Lithium-ion secondary (rechargeable) cell:
• Positive electrode: Li<sup>+</sup> + CoO<sub>2</sub> + e<sup>−</sup> → Li<sup>+</sup>[CoO<sub>2</sub>]<sup>−</sup>.
• Negative electrode: Li → Li<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>−</sup>.
Alkaline Hydrogen-Oxygen Fuel Cell:
• Negative electrode (anode): 2H2 + 4OH− → 4H2O + 4e−.
• Positive electrode (cathode): O2 + 2H2O + 4e− → 4OH−.
• Overall: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O (E° = +1.23 V).
Advantages: Only water produced (zero emissions at point of use), higher energy efficiency than combustion.
Disadvantages: Hydrogen storage under high pressure, hydrogen currently made from fossil methane.

3.1.12.title: Topic 3.1.12 · Acids, Bases & Buffers (A-Level)
3.1.12.spec: Brønsted-Lowry theory, pH, Kw, weak acids Ka, titration curves, indicators, buffer solutions

sections.heading: pH, Kw & Strong Acids/Bases
points: Brønsted-Lowry: Acid = proton donor; Base = proton acceptor.
pH definition: pH = −log10[H+] → [H+] = 10−pH. (Report pH to 2 decimal places!).
Strong monoprotic acid: Fully dissociated, so [H+] = [acid].

Ionic product of water (Kw): Kw = [H+][OH−] = 1.00 × 10−14 mol2 dm−6 at 298 K. Dissociation is endothermic, so Kw increases as T increases → pure water pH < 7 at higher T (still neutral as [H+] = [OH−]).
Strong base calculation: [H+] = Kw / [OH−] → pH = −log10[H+].

sections.heading: Weak Acids (Ka) & Titration Curves
points: Acid dissociation constant (Ka): Ka = ([H+][A−]) / [HA]. pKa = −log10Ka.
Weak acid approximation: [H+] = √(Ka × c).
Half-neutralisation point: When [HA] = [A−], pH = pKa.
Indicators: Change colour over pH range matching the vertical equivalence steep section:
• Strong acid - Strong base: Vertical pH 3–9. Methyl orange or Phenolphthalein.
• Weak acid - Strong base: Vertical pH 7–10. Phenolphthalein (colourless to pink).
• Strong acid - Weak base: Vertical pH 3–7. Methyl orange (red to yellow).
• Weak acid - Weak base: No sharp vertical break; use pH meter.

sections.heading: Buffer Solutions
points: Definition: A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added.
Acidic buffer: Weak acid + salt of that weak acid (e.g. CH3COOH and CH3COONa).
• Adding H+: Reacts with salt anion: A− + H+ → HA.
• Adding OH−: Reacts with weak acid: HA + OH− → A− + H2O.
Buffer calculation: [H+] = Ka × ([acid] / [salt]).

3.2.1.title: Topic 3.2.1 · Periodicity
3.2.1.spec: Classification of elements in s, p, d, f blocks; Period 3 trends in atomic radius, first IE, and melting point

sections.heading: Classification & Period 3 Trends
points: Blocks: Elements classified into s, p, d, or f block depending on the sub-shell containing the highest energy electron.

Atomic radius across Period 3: Decreases from Na to Cl. Nuclear charge increases while shielding remains approximately constant; stronger electrostatic attraction pulls outer electrons closer to the nucleus.
First Ionisation Energy across Period 3: General increase due to increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius.
• Dip at Al (Group 3): Outer electron is in 3p subshell, which is higher in energy and partially shielded by 3s electrons.
• Dip at S (Group 6): Electron pair in one 3p orbital causes spin-pair repulsion, making the electron easier to remove than from phosphorus (half-filled 3p3).

sections.heading: Melting Point Trends Across Period 3
points: Na, Mg, Al (Metallic bonding): Melting points increase. Ionic charge increases (Na+ < Mg2+ < Al3+), ionic radius decreases, and number of delocalised electrons per atom increases (1 → 2 → 3), leading to stronger metallic bonds.
Si (Giant macromolecular covalent): Highest melting point in Period 3. Many strong tetrahedral covalent bonds throughout 3D giant lattice require enormous energy to break.

P4, S8, Cl2, Ar (Simple molecular): Melting points depend strictly on the strength of van der Waals (London dispersion) forces between molecules, which depend on molecular size / number of electrons: S8 (highest) > P4 > Cl2 > Ar (lowest).

3.2.2.title: Topic 3.2.2 · Group 2, Alkaline Earth Metals
3.2.2.spec: Trends in atomic radius, first IE, melting point, reactivity with water; solubilities of hydroxides and sulfates; uses

sections.heading: Group 2 Trends & Reactions with Water
points: Trends down Group 2 (Mg to Ba): Atomic radius increases; first & second ionisation energies decrease; reactivity with water increases.
Reaction with water:
• Mg with cold water: Very slow: Mg + 2H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2 + H2.
• Mg with steam: Rapid, white flame, white ash: Mg(s) + H2O(g) → MgO(s) + H2(g).
• Ca, Sr, Ba: React with increasing vigour with cold water to form alkaline hydroxide solutions and effervescence of H2.

sections.heading: Solubility Trends & Real-World Uses
points: Hydroxides (M(OH)2): Solubility INCREASES down the group.
• Mg(OH)2: Sparingly soluble. Used in medicine as Milk of Magnesia (antacid for indigestion; OH− neutralises stomach acid; safe because low solubility prevents harmful high pH).
• Ca(OH)2: Partially soluble (slaked lime). Used in agriculture to neutralise acidic soils.
Sulfates (MSO4): Solubility DECREASES down the group.
• BaSO4: Completely insoluble. Used as Barium meal in medicine for X-ray imaging of digestive tract (safe despite toxic Ba2+ because its extreme insolubility prevents absorption into bloodstream).
Test for Sulfate ions: Add dilute HCl (to remove interfering CO32− ions), then add BaCl2(aq). Positive result: thick white precipitate of BaSO4.
Extraction of Titanium: Mg acts as reducing agent: TiCl4 + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl2 (high temp, argon atmosphere).
Flue Gas Desulfurisation: CaO or CaCO3 slurry sprayed into chimney emissions to react with acidic SO2: CaO + SO2 → CaSO3.

3.2.3.title: Topic 3.2.3 · Group 7(17), The Halogens
3.2.3.spec: Trends in electronegativity, boiling point, oxidising and reducing abilities; halide tests with silver nitrate and ammonia; chlorine chemistry

sections.heading: Trends in Physical Properties & Oxidising Power
points: Electronegativity: Decreases down group (F > Cl > Br > I) due to increased shielding and atomic radius.
Boiling points: Increase down group (F2 gas < Cl2 gas < Br2 liquid < I2 solid) due to stronger van der Waals forces between larger molecules.
Oxidising ability: DECREASES down group (Cl2 > Br2 > I2). Fluorine is the most powerful oxidiser.
• Cl<sub>2</sub> displaces Br<sup>−</sup> (orange solution formed) and I<sup>−</sup> (brown solution formed).
• Br<sub>2</sub> displaces I<sup>−</sup> only.
• I<sub>2</sub> displaces neither.

sections.heading: Reducing Ability of Halides with Conc H2SO4
points: Reducing power: INCREASES down group: F− < Cl− < Br− < I− (larger ionic radius, electron more easily lost).
• NaCl + H2SO4: Acid-base only: NaCl + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HCl (steamy fumes of HCl). No redox.
• NaBr + H2SO4: Redox occurs: forms orange fumes of Br2 and choking toxic gas SO2 (sulfur reduced from +6 to +4).
• NaI + H2SO4: Powerful reduction: forms purple fumes / black solid of I2, choking SO2, yellow solid sulfur S (+6 to 0), and rotten-egg gas H2S (+6 to −2).

sections.heading: Halide Ion Testing & Disproportionation of Chlorine
points: Testing for Halides: Acidify with dilute HNO3 (removes CO32− or OH− which would form false ppts), then add AgNO3(aq):
• Chloride (Cl−): White precipitate (AgCl). Dissolves in dilute NH3.
• Bromide (Br−): Cream precipitate (AgBr). Insoluble in dilute NH3; dissolves in concentrated NH3.
• Iodide (I−): Yellow precipitate (AgI). Insoluble in concentrated NH3.
Disproportionation of Chlorine:
• With water (water treatment): Cl2 + H2O ⇌ HClO + HCl. Chloric(I) acid (HClO) sterilises drinking water. Health benefits far outweigh toxic risks.
• In sunlight: 2Cl2 + 2H2O → 4HCl + O2.
• With cold dilute NaOH (bleach): Cl2 + 2NaOH → NaClO + NaCl + H2O (sodium chlorate(I) is active bleach).

3.2.4.title: Topic 3.2.4 · Period 3 Elements & Their Oxides (A-Level)
3.2.4.spec: Reactions of Period 3 with O2, structures, melting points, reactions with water and pH, acidic/basic/amphoteric behavior

sections.heading: Oxides Formation, Structures & Melting Points
points: Reactions with Oxygen:
• 2Na + ½O<sub>2</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>O (yellow flame, white solid)
• Mg + ½O<sub>2</sub> → MgO (brilliant white flame, white solid)
• 4Al + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (bright white sparks)
• Si + O<sub>2</sub> → SiO<sub>2</sub> (slow reaction)
• P<sub>4</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> (vigorous white flame, dense white smoke)
• S + O<sub>2</sub> → SO<sub>2</sub> (blue flame, choking gas); 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub>

Structure & mp: Na2O, MgO, Al2O3 have giant ionic lattices (high mp; MgO highest due to Mg2+ and O2− high charge density). SiO2 is giant covalent (very high mp). P4O10, SO2, SO3 are simple molecular with weak van der Waals (low mp).

sections.heading: Reactions with Water & Acid-Base Character
points: Reactions with Water:
• Na<sub>2</sub>O(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) (strongly alkaline, pH ~14)
• MgO(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) ⇌ Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>(aq) (sparingly soluble, pH ~9)
• Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and SiO<sub>2</sub>: Insoluble in water due to high lattice/covalent energy (pH 7).
• P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>(s) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O(l) → 4H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>(aq) (phosphoric(V) acid, pH 0–1)
• SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) ⇌ H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>(aq) (sulfuric(IV) acid, pH 2–3)
• SO<sub>3</sub>(l) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l) → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq) (sulfuric(VI) acid, pH 0)
Amphoteric nature of Al2O3:
• Acts as base: Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 6HCl → 2AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
• Acts as acid: Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 2NaOH + 3H<sub>2</sub>O → 2Na[Al(OH)<sub>4</sub>]

3.2.5.title: Topic 3.2.5 · Transition Metals (A-Level)
3.2.5.spec: Transition metal characteristics, complexes, ligands, isomerism, origin of colour, variable oxidation states, catalysts

sections.heading: Characteristics & Ligand Substitution
points: Definition: A transition element forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d sub-level (Sc and Zn are not transition metals).
Properties: Variable oxidation states, complex formation, coloured ions, catalytic activity.
Ligands: Monodentate (H2O, NH3, Cl−), Bidentate (1,2-diaminoethane 'en', C2O42−), Multidentate (EDTA4−, haem).
Chelate Effect: Substitution of monodentate ligands by multidentate ligands produces more product particles than reactants → ΔS is positive → ΔG < 0, making the complex far more stable.

Shapes of complexes: Octahedral (6-coord with small ligands H2O, NH3, 90°), Tetrahedral (4-coord with large Cl−, 109.5° e.g. [CuCl4]2−), Square planar (cisplatin [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]), Linear (Tollens' [Ag(NH3)2]+).

sections.heading: Coloured Ions & Catalysis
points: Origin of Colour: Ligands cause 3d orbitals to split into two different energy levels. Electrons absorb specific frequencies of visible light (ΔE = hν = hc/λ) to promote an electron from ground state to excited state. Transmitted/reflected light is the complementary colour.
Factors affecting colour (ΔE): Central metal ion, oxidation state, coordination number, and ligand identity.
Catalysts:
• Heterogeneous (Contact process): V2O5 + SO2 → V2O4 + SO3, then V2O4 + ½O2 → V2O5.
• Homogeneous (S2O82− + 2I−): Catalysed by Fe2+: S2O82− + 2Fe2+ → 2SO42− + 2Fe3+, then 2Fe3+ + 2I− → 2Fe2+ + I2.
• Autocatalysis (MnO4− + C2O42−): Mn2+ ions produced catalyse the reaction.

3.2.6.title: Topic 3.2.6 · Reactions of Ions in Aqueous Solution (A-Level)
3.2.6.spec: Metal-aqua ions, acidity of 2+ vs 3+ ions, test-tube reactions with NaOH, NH3, and Na2CO3

sections.heading: Acidity of Metal-Aqua Ions
points: Metal-aqua ions: [Fe(H2O)6]2+ (pale green), [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (blue), [Fe(H2O)6]3+ (purple/yellow-brown), [Al(H2O)6]3+ (colourless).

Why 3+ ions are more acidic than 2+ ions: 3+ ions have a higher charge and smaller ionic radius (greater charge/size ratio). They polarise the O−H bonds in coordinated water molecules more strongly, weakening the O−H bond and releasing H+ into solution.

sections.heading: Test-Tube Observations (Essential Summary Table)
points: [Fe(H2O)6]2+: +NaOH → green ppt Fe(H2O)4(OH)2 (turns brown in air). +excess NH3 → green ppt (insoluble in excess). +Na2CO3 → green ppt of FeCO3 (no gas).
[Cu(H2O)6]2+: +NaOH → blue ppt Cu(H2O)4(OH)2. +excess NH3 → deep blue solution [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+. +Na2CO3 → blue-green ppt of CuCO3 (no gas).
[Fe(H2O)6]3+: +NaOH → brown ppt Fe(H2O)3(OH)3. +NH3 → brown ppt. +Na2CO3 → brown ppt AND effervescence of CO2 gas (3+ ion is acidic enough to liberate CO2 from carbonate).

[Al(H2O)6]3+: +NaOH → white ppt Al(H2O)3(OH)3; redissolves in excess NaOH to colourless [Al(OH)4]− (amphoteric!). +NH3 → white ppt (insoluble in excess). +Na2CO3 → white ppt AND effervescence of CO2 gas.

3.3.1.title: Topic 3.3.1 · Introduction to Organic Chemistry
3.3.1.spec: Nomenclature, formulas (empirical, molecular, structural, displayed, skeletal), curly arrow mechanisms, isomerism (structural, E/Z, CIP rules)

sections.heading: Formulas & IUPAC Rules
points: Formulas: Empirical (simplest ratio), Molecular (actual count), General (e.g. CnH2n+2), Structural (e.g. CH3CH2OH), Displayed (all bonds and atoms shown), Skeletal (carbon backbone zigzag, heteroatoms and functional groups explicitly shown).

IUPAC Nomenclature: Identify longest continuous carbon chain (stem: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex); number chain from end giving lowest locator numbers to functional groups; list substituents alphabetically (ignoring di-, tri- prefixes).

sections.heading: Reaction Mechanisms & Isomerism
points: Curly arrows: Always represent the movement of an electron pair. Starts at a lone pair or covalent bond; points to an electron-deficient atom or the site where a new bond is formed.
Structural Isomerism: Same molecular formula, different structural formula:
• Chain: Different carbon skeleton arrangement.
• Position: Same functional group at different positions on carbon skeleton.
• Functional group: Different functional group (e.g. alkene vs cycloalkane, alcohol vs ether, aldehyde vs ketone, carboxylic acid vs ester).
Stereoisomerism: Same structural formula, different arrangement of atoms in 3D space.

E/Z Isomerism: Arises from restricted rotation about planar C=C double bond, and each C atom having two different groups attached. Cahn-Ingold-Prelog (CIP) priority: Higher atomic number gets higher priority on each double-bonded carbon. Z = high priority on same side (z-zame zide); E = high priority on opposite sides.

3.3.2.title: Topic 3.3.2 · Alkanes
3.3.2.spec: Fractional distillation of crude oil, cracking, combustion, pollution, free-radical chlorination mechanism

sections.heading: Fractional Distillation & Cracking
points: Alkanes: Saturated hydrocarbons with general formula CnH2n+2. Non-polar, held by weak van der Waals forces.
Fractional distillation: Fractionating column has temperature gradient (hot at bottom, cool at top). Hydrocarbons vaporised; separate by boiling point (smaller molecules condense near top).
Thermal Cracking: High temperature (700–1200 K) and high pressure (up to 7000 kPa). Produces high percentage of alkenes (used for polymers).
Catalytic Cracking: Slight pressure, high temperature (720 K), zeolite catalyst. Produces branched alkanes, cycloalkanes, and aromatic hydrocarbons (used for motor fuels).

sections.heading: Combustion & Free-Radical Substitution
points: Pollutants: Complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O. Incomplete combustion gives toxic CO and carbon soot. High temperatures in internal combustion engines cause N2 and O2 to react forming NOx.
Catalytic converters: Platinum/rhodium catalyst: 2NO + 2CO → N2 + 2CO2.
Free-Radical Substitution of Methane (CH4 + Cl2):
• Initiation: Cl2 → 2Cl• (homolytic fission triggered by UV light).
• Propagation 1: Cl• + CH4 → •CH3 + HCl.
• Propagation 2: •CH3 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl•.
• Termination: •CH3 + Cl• → CH3Cl; •CH3 + •CH3 → C2H6; Cl• + Cl• → Cl2.

3.3.3.title: Topic 3.3.3 · Halogenoalkanes
3.3.3.spec: Nucleophilic substitution mechanisms, bond enthalpy vs polarity, elimination reactions, ozone depletion by CFCs

sections.heading: Nucleophilic Substitution Mechanisms
points: Polar C−X bond: Carbon has partial positive charge (δ+) attacked by electron-rich nucleophiles.
• Warm aqueous NaOH: Nucleophile :OH− replaces X to form alcohols.
• Ethanolic KCN: Nucleophile :CN− forms nitriles (extends carbon chain by one carbon atom).
• Excess ethanolic NH3 under pressure: Nucleophile :NH3 forms primary amines (excess NH3 prevents further substitution).
Reactivity order: R−I > R−Br > R−Cl > R−F. The C−I bond enthalpy is the lowest and easiest to break, so iodoalkanes react fastest regardless of bond polarity.

sections.heading: Elimination vs Substitution & Ozone Layer
points: Elimination: Reagent: hot ethanolic KOH. The OH− acts as a base, abstracting a proton from an adjacent carbon atom, forming an alkene + H2O + X−.
Condition comparison: Aqueous + warm → substitution. Ethanolic + hot reflux → elimination.
Ozone Depletion by CFCs:
• UV photolysis: CF2Cl2 → •CF2Cl + Cl•
• Catalytic destruction: Cl• + O3 → ClO• + O2 and ClO• + O3 → Cl• + 2O2 (overall 2O3 → 3O2). Chlorine radicals are regenerated to destroy thousands of ozone molecules.

3.3.4.title: Topic 3.3.4 · Alkenes
3.3.4.spec: Electrophilic addition reactions with HBr, H2SO4, Br2; carbocation stabilities, addition polymers

sections.heading: Electrophilic Addition Reactions & Mechanisms
points: Reactivity: C=C double bond consists of a σ bond and an exposed π bond of high electron density, attracting electrophiles.
• With Br2: Induced dipole on Br2. Carbocation intermediate formed. Forms 1,2-dibromoalkane. Bromine water test: Orange to colourless confirms unsaturation.
• With HBr: Forms bromoalkane.
• With conc H2SO4: Forms alkyl hydrogen sulfate, which upon adding water and warming hydrolyses to an alcohol (regeneration of H2SO4 catalyst).

Major vs Minor Products (Markovnikov's Rule): In unsymmetrical alkenes, the electrophile H+ attaches to the carbon with more hydrogens, creating the more stable carbocation intermediate (stability: tertiary > secondary > primary due to positive inductive effect of alkyl groups).

sections.heading: Addition Polymers
points: Formation: Alkenes join together with no other product. π bond breaks to link monomer units.

Poly(chloroethene) (PVC): Rigid and waterproof; used for drainpipes and window frames. Addition of plasticisers pushes chains apart, allowing them to slide, making PVC flexible (used for electrical cable insulation and clothing).
Properties: Saturated non-polar carbon backbone makes polyalkenes chemically inert and non-biodegradable.

3.3.5.title: Topic 3.3.5 · Alcohols
3.3.5.spec: Industrial production (fermentation vs hydration), biofuels, oxidation of alcohols, elimination/dehydration

sections.heading: Production of Ethanol & Biofuels
points: 1. Hydration of Ethene: CH2=CH2 + H2O(g) ⇌ CH3CH2OH. Conditions: conc H3PO4 catalyst, 300°C, 60 atm. Continuous, pure product, fast, but uses non-renewable crude oil.
2. Fermentation of Glucose: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2. Conditions: yeast enzyme, 35°C, anaerobic. Batch process, slow, impure (needs fractional distillation), but uses renewable sugar cane/corn.
Biofuel & Carbon Neutrality:
• Photosynthesis: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub> (absorbs 6 CO<sub>2</sub>).
• Fermentation: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2CO<sub>2</sub> (releases 2 CO<sub>2</sub>).
• Combustion: 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 6O<sub>2</sub> → 4CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (releases 4 CO<sub>2</sub>).
• Theoretically zero net CO2, but in practice not carbon neutral due to fossil fuels burned in transport, farming machinery, fertiliser production, and distillation.

sections.heading: Oxidation & Elimination of Alcohols
points: Oxidising agent: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4). Orange Cr2O72− reduced to green Cr3+.
• Primary alcohol: Distil off immediately → Aldehyde. Reflux with excess oxidiser → Carboxylic acid.
• Secondary alcohol: Reflux → Ketone.
• Tertiary alcohol: Cannot be oxidised (no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the −OH group; solution stays orange).
Elimination (Dehydration): Heat with conc H2SO4 or conc H3PO4 at 170°C: Alcohol → Alkene + H2O. (Produces addition polymers without crude oil).

3.3.6.title: Topic 3.3.6 · Organic Analysis
3.3.6.spec: Functional group test-tube reactions, high resolution mass spectrometry, infrared spectroscopy

sections.heading: Chemical Tests for Functional Groups
points: • Alkene: Shake with bromine water → Orange to colourless.
• Halogenoalkane: Warm with aqueous NaOH, acidify with HNO3, add AgNO3 → AgCl white ppt, AgBr cream ppt, AgI yellow ppt.
• 1° and 2° Alcohol: Warm with acidified K2Cr2O7 → Orange to green.
• Aldehyde vs Ketone:
- Tollens' reagent ([Ag(NH3)2]+): Warm → Silver mirror with aldehyde; no reaction with ketone.
- Fehling's solution: Warm → Blue solution to brick red precipitate (Cu2O) with aldehyde; stays blue with ketone.
• Carboxylic acid: Add Na2CO3(s) or NaHCO3(aq) → Effervescence of CO2 gas (turns limewater cloudy).

sections.heading: High-Res Mass Spectrometry & Infrared (IR) Spectroscopy
points: High Resolution MS: Measures molecular ion m/z to 4 or 5 decimal places. Enables distinguishing between molecules with identical integer masses (e.g. C3H6O = 58.0419 vs C4H10 = 58.0782) using precise isotopic masses.
Infrared Spectroscopy: Covalent bonds vibrate and absorb specific IR frequencies corresponding to bond wavenumber.
• O−H (alcohols): Broad absorption at 3230–3550 cm−1.
• O−H (carboxylic acids): Very broad absorption overlapping C−H at 2500–3000 cm−1.
• C=O (carbonyl): Strong sharp peak at 1680–1750 cm−1.
• C=C (alkene): Peak at 1620–1680 cm−1.
Fingerprint region (<1500 cm−1): Unique pattern of complex bending vibrations; compare against computer library to identify exact molecule and check purity.

3.3.7.title: Topic 3.3.7 · Optical Isomerism (A-Level)
3.3.7.spec: Asymmetric carbon atom, enantiomers, plane-polarised light, racemates

sections.heading: Chirality & Enantiomers
points: Chiral centre / Asymmetric carbon: A carbon atom bonded to four different groups/atoms (marked with an asterisk *C).
Optical isomers (enantiomers): Non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
Optical activity: Each enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light by equal angles in opposite directions (+ / clockwise and − / anticlockwise).
Racemic mixture (racemate): An equimolar (50:50) mixture of two enantiomers. It is optically inactive because the opposite rotations of each enantiomer cancel each other out.
Origin of racemates: Formed when planar trigonal groups (e.g. C=O carbonyl or planar carbocation) are attacked by a nucleophile from either face with equal 50% probability.

3.3.8.title: Topic 3.3.8 · Aldehydes & Ketones (A-Level)
3.3.8.spec: Nucleophilic addition reactions with NaBH4 and KCN, hazards of cyanide, mechanism

sections.heading: Nucleophilic Addition Mechanisms
points: Carbonyl group polarity: C=δ+ and O=δ−. The planar carbon is susceptible to nucleophilic attack.
1. Reduction using NaBH4 in aqueous solution:
• Nucleophile is hydride ion :H−.
• Aldehyde → Primary alcohol; Ketone → Secondary alcohol.
• Mechanism: :H<sup>−</sup> attacks C<sup>δ+</sup>, C=O π electron pair moves onto O; intermediate alkoxide attacks H<sup>δ+</sup> of H<sub>2</sub>O.
2. Addition of KCN followed by dilute acid:
• Forms a hydroxynitrile (2-hydroxyalkanenitrile). Useful in organic synthesis because it increases chain length by one carbon.
• Mechanism: :CN<sup>−</sup> attacks planar C=O; O<sup>−</sup> protonated by H<sup>+</sup>.
• Formation of racemic mixture: Planar C=O can be attacked by :CN− from above or below the plane with equal probability, producing equal amounts of enantiomers.
• Cyanide hazards: KCN is highly toxic. Acidification releases lethal HCN gas. Must use a fume cupboard.

3.3.9.title: Topic 3.3.9 · Carboxylic Acids & Derivatives (A-Level)
3.3.9.spec: Esterification, uses of esters, triglycerides, soap, biodiesel, acylation mechanisms with acyl chlorides and anhydrides

sections.heading: Esters, Fats & Biodiesel
points: Esterification: Carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ Ester + water (conc H2SO4 catalyst, heat under reflux). Sweet smelling, used in perfumes, solvents, food flavourings.
Hydrolysis of esters:
• Acid hydrolysis: Reflux with dilute acid ⇌ Carboxylic acid + alcohol (reversible).
• Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification): Reflux with aqueous NaOH → Carboxylate salt + alcohol (irreversible, higher yield).
Vegetable oils & fats: Triesters of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) and long-chain fatty acids. Alkaline hydrolysis produces soap (sodium salts of fatty acids) and glycerol.
Biodiesel: Mixture of methyl esters of fatty acids made by reacting vegetable oils with methanol using a KOH catalyst.

sections.heading: Acylation (Nucleophilic Addition-Elimination)
points: Acylating agents: Acyl chlorides (RCOCl) and Acid anhydrides ((RCO)2O).
Reactions with nucleophiles:
• + H<sub>2</sub>O → Carboxylic acid + HCl / RCOOH (steamy fumes)
• + Alcohol → Ester + HCl / RCOOH
• + NH<sub>3</sub> → Primary amide + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl / RCOONH<sub>4</sub>
• + Primary amine → N-substituted amide + R'NH<sub>3</sub>Cl
Manufacture of Aspirin: Salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) + ethanoic anhydride → Aspirin + ethanoic acid.
Why ethanoic anhydride is preferred industrially: Cheaper; less corrosive; slower and less violent reaction; does not produce dangerous toxic fumes of HCl gas.

3.3.10.title: Topic 3.3.10 · Aromatic Chemistry (A-Level)
3.3.10.spec: Structure and bonding of benzene, enthalpy of hydrogenation evidence, electrophilic substitution (nitration, Friedel-Crafts)

sections.heading: Structure & Stability of Benzene
points: Benzene structure: Planar hexagonal ring (C6H6). Each C is bonded to 2 other carbons and 1 hydrogen. The remaining p orbital on each carbon overlaps sideways to form a delocalised π electron system above and below the ring. All carbon-carbon bond lengths are identical (0.139 nm, between single and double).
Thermochemical evidence for delocalisation:
• Enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.
• Theoretical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene (Kekulé model) would be 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.
• Experimental enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is only −208 kJ mol−1.
• Benzene is 152 kJ mol−1 more stable than predicted due to delocalisation energy.

sections.heading: Electrophilic Substitution Mechanisms
points: Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition in order to preserve its stable aromatic π system.
1. Nitration:
• Electrophile generation: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 → NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+.
• Electrophile is the nitronium ion (NO2+).
• Maintain temperature below 55°C to prevent multiple substitutions.
• Nitrobenzene is reduced to phenylamine for azo dye manufacture.
2. Friedel-Crafts Acylation:
• Electrophile generation: RCOCl + AlCl3 → RCO+ + AlCl4− (AlCl3 is a Lewis acid catalyst).
• Electrophile is acylium ion (RCO<sup>+</sup>). Product is an aromatic ketone.
• Catalyst regeneration: AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → AlCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl.

3.3.11.title: Topic 3.3.11 · Amines (A-Level)
3.3.11.spec: Preparation of amines, base properties, nucleophilic substitution with haloalkanes, cationic surfactants

sections.heading: Preparation & Base Strength
points: Preparation:
• From halogenoalkanes: Warm with excess ethanolic NH3 under pressure.
• Reduction of nitriles: R−CN + 4[H] → R−CH2NH2 using LiAlH4 in dry ether or H2 / Ni catalyst.
• Aromatic amines: Reduce nitrobenzene using tin (Sn) and concentrated HCl, then add NaOH to release free phenylamine.
Base Strength (lone pair availability on N):
• Secondary aliphatic > Primary aliphatic > Ammonia > Aromatic amine.
• Alkyl groups have positive inductive effect (+I), pushing electron density onto N, making lone pair more available to accept H<sup>+</sup>.
• In phenylamine, the N lone pair delocalises into the aromatic π ring, drastically reducing availability to accept protons.

sections.heading: Amines as Nucleophiles & Cationic Surfactants
points: Successive substitution: 1° amine reacts with haloalkane → 2° amine → 3° amine → quaternary ammonium salt [R4N]+X−.

Cationic Surfactants: Quaternary ammonium salts with a long hydrocarbon tail and positive head. Positive head attracts negative surfaces (hair, fabrics), tail points outward, reducing static friction. Used in fabric softeners and hair conditioners.

3.3.12.title: Topic 3.3.12 · Polymers (A-Level)
3.3.12.spec: Condensation polymers (polyesters, polyamides), repeating units, intermolecular forces, disposal & biodegradability

sections.heading: Condensation Polymers
points: Condensation polymerisation: Monomers join with the elimination of a small molecule (usually H2O or HCl).
1. Polyesters: Formed from dicarboxylic acid + diol (or hydroxycarboxylic acid).
• Terylene (PET): Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid + ethane-1,2-diol. Linkage: ester (−COO−). Used in clothing and drink bottles.
2. Polyamides: Formed from dicarboxylic acid + diamine (or amino acid).
• Nylon 6,6: Hexanedioic acid + hexane-1,6-diamine. Linkage: peptide/amide (−CONH−). Used in ropes and carpets.
• Kevlar: Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid + benzene-1,4-diamine. Strong rigid chains with extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding; used in bulletproof vests and fire protection gear.

sections.heading: Disposal & Biodegradability
points: Addition polymers (polyalkenes): Non-polar, chemically inert C−C backbone. Non-biodegradable; persist in landfills for centuries.
Condensation polymers: Contain polar ester and amide bonds susceptible to hydrolysis by acid or alkali; they are biodegradable.
Recycling: Reduces landfill waste and conserves fossil fuels, but requires sorting and cleaning, which is labour intensive and costly.

3.3.13.title: Topic 3.3.13 · Amino Acids, Proteins & DNA (A-Level)
3.3.13.spec: Amino acid zwitterions, peptide links, protein structure, enzymes, DNA structure and base pairing, cisplatin anticancer drug

sections.heading: Amino Acids & Zwitterions
points: Structure: 2-amino acids contain both −NH2 and −COOH on the same carbon: H2N−CHR−COOH.
Zwitterion: Dipolar ion formed by internal acid-base transfer: +H3N−CHR−COO−. High melting points due to ionic attraction.
• In acidic solution (low pH): −COO− gains H+ → cation +H3N−CHR−COOH.
• In alkaline solution (high pH): +H3N− loses H+ → anion H2N−CHR−COO−.

sections.heading: Proteins, Enzymes, DNA & Cisplatin
points: Protein structure: Primary (amino acid sequence), Secondary (α-helix and β-pleated sheets stabilized by hydrogen bonds), Tertiary (3D folding stabilized by H-bonds, ionic bonds, and disulfide −S−S− bridges).
Enzymes: Protein catalysts with stereospecific active sites that bind only one optical enantiomer of a substrate. Drugs act as competitive inhibitors.

DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid): Nucleotide = phosphate group + 2-deoxyribose + base (A, T, C, G). Two complementary anti-parallel strands in double helix held by hydrogen bonds between base pairs: A pairs with T (2 H-bonds); C pairs with G (3 H-bonds).

Cisplatin: Platinum(II) complex [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]. Acts as anticancer drug: undergoes ligand substitution with N atom on guanine in DNA, kinking the DNA double helix and preventing replication. Side effects: hair loss and kidney damage.

3.3.14.title: Topic 3.3.14 · Organic Synthesis (A-Level)
3.3.14.spec: Designing multi-step synthetic routes (up to 4 steps), atom economy, avoiding hazardous solvents

sections.heading: Synthetic Strategy & Green Chemistry
points: Multi-step strategy: Work backwards (retrosynthesis) identifying required functional group interconversions (FGIs).
Key synthetic interconversions:
• Alkene → Haloalkane (HX) → Nitrile (KCN) → Primary amine (LiAlH<sub>4</sub>) or Carboxylic acid (acid hydrolysis).
• Alcohol → Aldehyde / Ketone → Hydroxynitrile.
• Benzene → Nitrobenzene → Phenylamine → N-phenylethanamide.
Green chemistry goals: Maximize atom economy, minimize number of reaction steps, avoid toxic solvents and reagents, use renewable feedstocks.

3.3.15.title: Topic 3.3.15 · NMR Spectroscopy (A-Level)
3.3.15.spec: 13C NMR, 1H NMR, chemical shift, integration, splitting patterns (n+1 rule), TMS standard, solvents

sections.heading: Principles & Reference Standard
points: Tetramethylsilane (TMS): Standard reference assigned δ = 0 ppm. Inert, volatile (easily removed), produces a single sharp intense peak with 12 equivalent protons, non-toxic.
Solvents: Must not contain protons (1H). Commonly CDCl3 (deuterated chloroform) or CCl4.
13C NMR: Number of peaks = number of distinct carbon environments. Chemical shift (δ) indicates environment type (carbonyl C=O at 160–220 ppm).

sections.heading: 1H NMR Interpretation & Splitting (n+1 Rule)
points: 1. Number of peaks: Number of non-equivalent proton environments.
2. Chemical shift (δ): Type of environment (alkyl 0.5–2, −O−CH3 3.5–4, aromatic 7–8, aldehyde 9–10, carboxylic acid 10–12 ppm).
3. Integration trace: Ratio of protons in each environment.
4. Spin-spin splitting (n+1 rule): Peak splits into n+1 sub-peaks, where n is the number of non-equivalent protons on ADJACENT carbons:
• Singlet (0 neighbours), Doublet (1 neighbour), Triplet (2 neighbours), Quartet (3 neighbours).
• Protons on −OH and −NH typically do not split adjacent protons and appear as singlets.

3.3.16.title: Topic 3.3.16 · Chromatography (A-Level)
3.3.16.spec: Thin-layer chromatography (TLC), column chromatography (CC), gas chromatography (GC), Rf values, GC-MS

sections.heading: Chromatographic Principles & Techniques
points: Separation mechanism: Separation depends on the balance between solubility in the moving phase and retention/adsorption by the stationary phase.
• Thin-Layer Chromatography (TLC): Stationary phase is solid silica or alumina plate; mobile phase is liquid solvent. Retention factor: Rf = (distance by spot) / (distance by solvent front).
• Column Chromatography (CC): Used to purify and separate preparative quantities of mixtures. Stationary phase packed into glass column; solvent washes through.

• Gas Chromatography (GC): Stationary phase is liquid or solid coating in long capillary column; mobile phase is inert carrier gas (He, N2). Substances identified by retention time. Area under peak is proportional to quantity.
• GC-MS: GC separates components; MS immediately analyzes each to determine precise molecular mass and fragmentation pattern.

RP.title: Topic RP · Required Practicals 1 to 12
RP.spec: The 12 AQA Required Practicals: apparatus, volumetric techniques, enthalpy, rates, tests for ions, distillation, organic synthesis, electrochemistry, pH curves, TLC

sections.heading: Physical & Inorganic Practicals (RP1 – RP6)
points: RP1 (Titration): Make volumetric solution in volumetric flask (invert to mix), rinse burette and pipette with reagents, concordant titres within 0.10 cm3.

RP2 (Enthalpy): Polystyrene cup calorimeter, measure initial temp for 3 mins, mix at min 4, record temp every min to min 10. Extrapolate cooling curve back to min 4 to find true ΔT. Calculate q = mcΔT.
RP3 (Rates & Temp): Disappearing cross reaction (Na2S2O3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + SO2 + S + H2O). 1/time is proportional to rate. Plot ln(1/t) vs 1/T for Arrhenius.

RP4 (Qualitative Analysis): Test for Group 2 cations with NaOH/H2SO4; test for NH4+ with warm NaOH and damp red litmus (turns blue); test for halides with acidified AgNO3; test for SO42− with acidified BaCl2; test for CO32− with acid (CO2 turns limewater cloudy).
RP5 (Distillation): Distil ethanal from oxidation of ethanol using anti-bumping granules, thermometer bulb level with condenser side-arm, water in at bottom of condenser.
RP6 (Organic Tests): Alkene (bromine water), 1°/2° alcohol (acidified dichromate), aldehyde (Tollens' silver mirror / Fehling's red ppt), carboxylic acid (Na2CO3 effervescence).

sections.heading: A-Level Advanced Practicals (RP7 – RP12)
points: RP7 (Rate determination): Initial rate by clock reaction (e.g. iodine clock) or continuous monitoring (gas syringe volume vs time; tangent to curve gives rate).
RP8 (Electrochemical Cells): Clean metal strips with emery paper, degrease, potassium nitrate salt bridge connecting half-cells, high resistance voltmeter.
RP9 (pH Curves): Calibrate pH meter using standard buffer solutions (pH 4, 7, 10). Add base in small portions (0.2 cm3 near equivalence point), plot pH vs volume.
RP10 (Organic Synthesis & Purification):
• Liquid: Reflux, separating funnel (wash with NaHCO3 to remove acid, run off aqueous layer), dry with anhydrous CaCl2/MgSO4, redistil.

• Solid (Aspirin): Dissolve in minimum volume of hot solvent, hot filtration, cool to crystallise, Büchner vacuum filtration, wash with ice-cold solvent, dry in oven. Test purity with melting point apparatus (sharp mp matching literature indicates purity; impurities lower and broaden mp range).
RP11 (Transition Metal Ions): Test [Fe(H2O)6]2+, [Cu(H2O)6]2+, [Fe(H2O)6]3+, [Al(H2O)6]3+ with NaOH, NH3, and Na2CO3.
RP12 (Thin-Layer Chromatography): Spot mixture on pencil line above solvent level, develop in sealed chamber with solvent vapor, visualize with ninhydrin or UV light, calculate Rf values.
